[[File:Acacia-decurrens-catalina.jpg|thumb|Habit in California]]

'''''Acacia decurrens''''', commonly known as '''black wattle''', '''Sydney green wattle''' or '''early green wattle''' and other common names, is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to [[New South Wales]], Australia. It is a tall shrub to tree with [[Pinnation#Iteration of divisions|bipinnate]], dark green leaves, spherical heads of golden yellow flowers and thinly leathery [[Pod (fruit)|pods]]. 

Cultivated throughout Australia, ''Acacia decurrens'' has naturalised in other Australian states and introduced to many other countries.

== Description ==
''Acacia decurrens'' is a tall shrub or tree that typically grows to a height of up to {{cvt|10 or 25|m}} and has smooth or fissured greyish black or black bark. The branchlets have winged ridges {{cvt|0.5–2|mm}} wide and are more or less [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]].<ref name="FoA11"/> Young foliage tips are light green or yellowish. The leaves are dark green and arranged alternately, bipinnate on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|15–28|mm}} long with 3 to 13 pairs of [[Pinna (botany)|pinnae]], each with 15 to 45 pairs of linear, widely spaced [[Leaflet (botany)|pinnules]] {{cvt|5–15|mm}} long and {{cvt|0.4–0.8|mm}} wide on a [[rhachis]] {{cvt|20–120|mm}} long. There are [[Gland (botany)|glands]] at the base of all the pairs of the pinnae.<ref name="plantnet">{{cite web |last1=Kodela |first1=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia decurrens'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acacia~decurrens |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney |access-date=1 September 2025}}</ref><ref name="FoA">{{cite web |last1=Kodela |first1=Phillip G. |last2=Tindale |first2=Mary D. |last3=Kodela |first3=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia decurrens'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Acacia%20decurrens |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water: Canberra. |access-date=2 September 2025}}</ref><ref name="lucid">{{cite web |title=''Acacia decurrens'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/wattle/text/entities/acacia_decurrens.htm |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study |access-date=2 September 2025}}</ref><ref name="www">{{cite web |title=''Acacis decurrens'' |url=https://worldwidewattle.com/speciesgallery/decurrens.php |publisher=World Wide Wattle |access-date=2 September 2025}}</ref>

The flowers are borne in spherical head in elongated [[raceme]]s or in groups on the ends of branches on [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] {{cvt|3–7|mm}} long, each head {{cvt|4–7|mm}} in diameter with 20 to 32 yellow, bright yellow or golden yellow flowers. The seed pods are straight to slightly curved, more or less flat and straight sided, {{cvt|20–105|mm}} long, {{cvt|5–8.5|mm}} wide, thinly leathery and mostly slightly constricted between the seeds.<ref name="plantnet" /><ref name="FoA" /><ref name="lucid" /><ref name="www" /> The pods mature from November to January.<ref name="Benson1996">{{cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=Doug |last2=McDougall |first2=Lyn |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species Part 4: Dicotyledon family Fabaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |date=1996 |volume=4 |issue=4 |page=700 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/313069#page/175/mode/1up |access-date=2 September 2025}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
This species was first formally described in 1798 by German botanist [[Johann Christoph Wendland]] who gave it the name ''Mimosa decurrens'' in his ''Botanische Beobachtungen: nebst einigen neuen Gattungen und Arten''<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Mimosa decurrens'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/486176 |publisher=APNI|access-date=1 September 2025}}</ref><ref name="Wendl.">{{cite book |last1=Wendland |first1=Johann Christoph |title=Botanische Beobachtungen : nebst einigen neuen Gattungen und Arten |date=1798 |publisher=Bey den Gebrüdern Hahn |location=Hanover |pages=57–58 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/186583#page/65/mode/1up |access-date=1 September 2025}}</ref> before his countryman [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]] redescribed it in the genus ''[[Acacia]]'' as ''A. decurrens'' in 1806.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Acacia decurrens'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/466915 |publisher=APNI|access-date=1 September 2025}}</ref> In his description, Willdenow did not cite Wendland but instead a 1796 description by [[James Donn]].<ref name="Willd.">{{cite book |last1=Willdenow |first1=Carl Ludwig |title=Species Plantarum |edition=4 |volume=4 |series = 2|date=1806 |page=1072 |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/12439/?offset=#page=441&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q= |access-date=1 September 2025}}</ref> However, as Donn's description was a ''[[nomen nudum]]'', the proper citation is  ''Acacia decurrens'' Willd.<ref name="FoA11">{{cite encyclopedia | author =Kodela, Phillip G. | year = 2001| title = Acacia |editor1=Wilson, Annette |editor2=Orchard, Anthony E. | encyclopedia = [[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]] | volume = 11A, 11B, Part 1: Mimosaceae, Acacia | page = 240 | publisher = CSIRO Publishing / [[Australian Biological Resources Study]] | isbn = 978-0-643-06718-9}}</ref>

The [[specific epithet]] (''decurrens'') means 'running down', referring to the narrow ridges on the leaves that are continuous with the branchlets.<ref name="FoA" />

Queensland botanist [[Leslie Pedley|Les Pedley]] reclassified the species as ''Racosperma decurrens'' in 2003, when he proposed placing almost all Australian members of the genus into the new genus ''[[Racosperma]]''.<ref name="pedley">{{cite journal|last=Pedley|first=Les|date=2003|title=A synopsis of ''Racosperma'' C.Mart. (Leguminosae: Mimosoideae)|journal=Austrobaileya |volume=6|issue=3|pages=445–96|doi=10.5962/p.299681 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/281479#page/101/mode/1up|doi-access=free}}</ref> However, this name is treated as a [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] of its original name.<ref name="APC" />

Common names include green wattle, Sydney green wattle, early black wattle, early green wattle, black wattle, wattah<ref name="FoA" /> and boo'kerrikin in the local [[Tharawal language|Dharawal language]].<ref name="plantnet" /><ref name="bodkin" /> [[Joseph Maiden|Maiden]] noted that it was called ''wat-tah'' by the indigenous people of Cumberland (Parramatta) and Camden districts.<ref name=maiden90>{{cite book | author=Maiden, Joseph Henry |author-link=Joseph Maiden| url=http://adc.library.usyd.edu.au/data-2/p00111.pdf | page=50 | title=Wattles and Wattlebarks of New South Wales: being hints on the conservation and cultivation of wattles, together with particulars of their value | year=1890 | publisher= Charles Potter |location=Sydney }}</ref> Sydney wattle was a name coined by [[Ferdinand von Mueller|von Mueller]] and early settlers around Penrith called it green wattle. Feathery wattle was another early name.<ref name=maiden90/> It is also known as early green wattle in the Sydney basin, as it flowers in winter—earlier than similar species, such as Parramatta wattle (''[[Acacia parramattensis]]''), blueskin (''[[Acacia irrorata|A. irrorata]]'') and late black wattle (''[[Acacia mearnsii|A. mearnsii]]'').<ref name=Fairley>{{cite book |author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |page=118|location=Kenthurst, New South Wales |isbn=978-0-7318-1031-4}}</ref> It has attracted the vernacular name 'green cancer' in South Africa, where it has become weedy.<ref name="holliday">{{cite book|last=Holliday|first=Ivan|title=A Field Guide to Australian Trees|publisher=Hamlyn|date=1989|edition=2nd|page=14|isbn=978-0-947334-08-6|location=Port Melbourne, Victoria}}</ref>

Along with other bipinnate wattles, ''A. decurrens'' is classified in the [[Section (botany)|section]] ''Botrycephalae'' within the [[subgenus]] ''Phyllodineae'' in the [[genus]] ''Acacia''. An analysis of [[Genomic DNA|genomic]] and [[chloroplast DNA]] along with morphological characters found that the section is [[Polyphyly|polyphyletic]], though the close relationships of ''A. decurrens'' and many other species were unable to be resolved.<ref name="brown 1991">{{cite Q|Q30040847|author1=Brown, Gillian K. |author2=Ariati, Siti R. |author3=Murphy, Daniel J. |author4=Miller, Joseph T. H. |author5=Ladiges, Pauline Y.|author-link5=Pauline Ladiges}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Acacia decurrensDistMap265.png|thumb|Distribution of ''Acacia decurrens'' in Australia]]
''Acacia decurrens'' is native to the coast and tablelands of New South Wales and the [[Australian Capital Territory]] mainly south from the [[Hunter Valley]], and is common in the [[Sydney]] region. It grows in forest, woodland and heath, often on river banks.<ref name="plantnet" /> It is found in altitudes up to {{cvt|1000|m}} with rainfall between {{convert|700-1400|mm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} per year, and grows with trees such as grey gum (''[[Eucalyptus punctata]]'') and narrow-leaved ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus crebra|E. crebra]]'') in loamy soils derived mainly from [[Wianamatta Group|Wianamatta shale]] and sandstone.<ref name=Benson1996/>

It was extensively planted in New South Wales, and it is difficult to tell whether it is native or naturalised in areas near its native range.<ref name="Qldweed">{{cite web|url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/acacia_decurrens.htm|title=''Acacia decurrens''|last=The University of Queensland|date=2011|work=Weeds of Australia Biosecurity Queensland Edition|publisher=Queensland Government|access-date=23 February 2015}}</ref> The species became naturalised in other states of Australia, including [[Queensland]], [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]], [[Western Australia]] and [[Tasmania]] and has been introduced in other parts of the world, including India, Africa, California, South America, New Zealand and China.<ref name="PoWO">{{cite web |title=''Acacia decurrens'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:470138-1 |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=2 September 2025}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The dark brown or black seed is the main source of reproduction. They can be spread by ants or birds, and form a seedbank in the soil. Seedlings generally grow rapidly after bushfire, and the species can colonise disturbed areas.<ref name=Benson1996/> Trees can live for 15 to 50 years.<ref name=Benson1996/>

[[Sulphur-crested cockatoo]]s eat the unripe seed.<ref name=Benson1996/>

The foliage serves as food for the caterpillars of the double-spotted line blue (''[[Nacaduba biocellata]]''), moonlight jewel (''[[Hypochrysops delicia]]''),  imperial hairstreak (''[[Jalmenus evagoras]]''),  ictinus blue (''[[Jalmenus ictinus]]''), amethyst hairstreak (''[[Jalmenus icilius]]'') and silky hairstreak (''[[Silky hairstreak|Pseudalmenus chlorinda]]'').<ref name="Edwards01">{{cite book|author1=Edwards, E. D. |author2=Newland, J. |author3=Regan, L. |title=Lepidoptera|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|date=2001|volume=31: Hesperioidea, Papilionoidea |pages=172, 222, 264–65, 267, 270 |isbn=9780643067004|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iVHDuVVelGMC&q=Acacia+parramattensis&pg=PA498}}</ref>

The wood serves as food for larvae of the jewel beetle species ''[[Agrilus australasiae]]'', ''[[Cisseis cupripennis]]'' and ''[[Cisseis scabrosula|C. scabrosula]]''.<ref>{{cite book|last=Bellamy|first=C.L.|title=Coleoptera|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|date=2002|volume=29: Buprestoidea|pages=347, 369, 381|isbn=9780643069008|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DlhTRU0UIP8C&q=Acacia+parramattensis&pg=PA2}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Uses of ''Acacia decurrens'' include chemical products, environmental management, and wood. The flowers are edible and are used in [[fritter]]s.  An edible gum oozing from the tree's trunk can be used as a lesser-quality substitute for [[gum arabic]], for example in the production of fruit jelly. The bark contains about 37–40% [[tannin]]. The flowers are used to produce yellow [[dye]], and the seed pods are used to produce green dye.<ref>[http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Acacia+decurrens Plants for a Future Database]</ref>  An organic chemical compound called [[kaempferol]] gives the flowers of ''A. decurrens'' their color.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://users.lycaeum.org/~mulga/acacia/phyto.html |title=Lycaeum – Phytochemistry Intro |access-date=2007-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930154547/http://users.lycaeum.org/~mulga/acacia/phyto.html |archive-date=2007-09-30 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It has been grown for firewood, or as a fast-growing windbreak or shelter tree.<ref name=EJ/>

[[Image:Acde 001 lhp.jpg|thumb|250px|Seeds]]

===Cultural significance===
In the [[Dharawal]] story of the Boo'kerrikin Sisters, one of the kindly sisters was turned into ''Acacia decurrens''. The other two sisters were turned into ''[[Acacia parvipinnula|A. parvipinnula]]'' and ''[[Acacia parramattensis|A. parramattensis]]''.<ref name=bodkin>{{cite web |last1=Bodkin |first1=Frances  |author-link1=Frances Bodkin |last2=Bodkin-Andrews |first2=Gawaian |date=2011|title=Doo'ragai Diday Boo'Kerrikin: The Sisters Boo'kerrikin |url=https://dharawalstories.files.wordpress.com/2018/05/bookerrikin-text.pdf |website=D'harawal DREAMING STORIES|location=Sydney}}</ref>  The flowering of ''A. decurrens'' was used as a [[Indigenous Australian seasons|seasonal indicator]] of the ceasing of cold winds and the beginning of a period of gentle rain.<ref>{{cite web |title=D'harawal calendar |url=http://www.bom.gov.au/iwk/calendars/dharawal.shtml |website=Indigenous Weather Knowledge |publisher=Bureau of Meteorology |access-date=22 April 2022 |date=2016}}</ref>

== Use in horticulture ==
''Acacia decurrens'' adapts easily to cultivation and grows very quickly. It can be used as a shelter or specimen tree in large gardens and parks.<ref name=EJ>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 2|year=1985|page=40 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne, Victoria |isbn=978-0-85091-143-5}}</ref> The tree can look imposing when in flower.<ref name="holliday"/> Cultivation of ''A. decurrens'' can be started by soaking the seeds in warm water and sowing them outdoors. The seeds keep their ability to germinate for many years.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_CfDcl2m-6BMC/page/n18 <!-- quote="acacia longifolia" uses. --> Internet Archive] ''Select Extra-tropical Plants Readily Eligible for Industrial Culture Or Naturalization'' By Ferdinand von Mueller</ref>

Fieldwork conducted in the Southern Highlands found that the presence of bipinnate wattles (either as understory or tree) was related to reduced numbers of [[noisy miner]]s, an aggressive species of bird that drives off small birds from gardens and bushland, and hence recommended the use of these plants in establishing [[wildlife corridor|green corridors]] and revegetation projects.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Hastings, Richard A. |author2=Beattie, Andrew J. |date=2006|title=Stop the bullying in the corridors: Can including shrubs make your revegetation more Noisy Miner free? |journal=Ecological Management & Restoration|volume=7|issue=2|pages=105–12|doi=10.1111/j.1442-8903.2006.00264.x|bibcode=2006EcoMR...7..105H }}</ref>
